title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $3.97: x0.85 and x0.60; noise-adjusted estimate of price effect is x0.72 vs baseline.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.1. The price is raised to $3.97 (+3.7% vs $3.83), and no events or promotions are scheduled. Past promotions show a noise-adjusted lift of x1.82, but this is a price increase, not a discount. The only relevant past data is a $3.97 price week (2026-09-28) with 106 units (x0.85 vs baseline), and another (2026-10-05) with 75 units (x0.60). These suggest a price increase causes demand to drop. The noise-adjusted effect of a $3.97 price is x0.72 vs baseline. No event or promotion is planned, so the classical model's 1.00 is misleading. We adjust down based on price effect evidence. Confidence is medium due to limited data on price spikes.

brief:
PRODUCT: Tortilla Chips 300g | category Snacks | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.1 | 5%-95%: 77.2 - 200.6 | 10%-90%: 88.7 - 170.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
